b2-optative.title: Let Me / Let's / May He: The Optative-Jussive
b2-optative.explanation: Turkish has a dedicated mood for suggestions, permission-seeking, and third-person wishes or commands. -(y)AyIm means 'let me...': 'Yardım edeyim' (Let me help). -(y)AlIm means 'let's...': 'Gidelim' (Let's go). -sIn means 'let him/may he...' or a polite third-person command: 'Biraz beklesin' (Let him wait a bit) or 'Herkes mutlu olsun' (May everyone be happy).
b2-optative.fact: Because -(y)AlIm and -(y)AyIm start with a vowel, they trigger the same p/ç/t/k softening you already know from -Iyor and -EcEk: gitmek becomes gidelim (let's go), not gitelim.

b2-past-necessity.title: Should Have: -mAlIydI
b2-past-necessity.explanation: -mAlI already expresses 'should' in the present/future. Add the past copula -(y)DI to shift it into regret about the past: 'Gitmeliydim' (I should have gone). Negate the -mAlI part, not the copula, for 'shouldn't have': 'Gitmemeliydim' (I shouldn't have gone).
b2-past-necessity.fact: -mAlIydI doesn't tell you by itself whether the action happened or not — context does. 'Erken kalkmalıydım' usually implies you didn't (a missed obligation), but it can also just mean 'it would have been proper' without specifying the outcome.

dialogue.en: You're right, I should have left earlier.

b2-o-kadar-ki.title: So...That: o kadar...ki
b2-o-kadar-ki.explanation: To say something is 'so X that Y,' put o kadar before the adjective or adverb and follow the whole sentence with ki plus the result: 'O kadar yorgundum ki hemen uyudum' (I was so tired that I fell asleep immediately). ki also appears after verbs of knowing/believing/hoping as a lighter, more conversational alternative to a -DIk noun clause: 'Biliyorum ki haklısın' (I know that you're right).
b2-o-kadar-ki.fact: ki is a borrowed Persian conjunction, one of the only common Turkish words that doesn't obey vowel harmony at all — it's always ki, never kı/kü/ku, no matter what precedes it.

dialogue.tr: O kadar çok trafik vardı ki iki saat yolda kaldım.
dialogue.en: There was so much traffic that I was stuck on the road for two hours.

b2-cause-clauses.title: Because: -DIğI için, dolayı, yüzünden
b2-cause-clauses.pattern: -DIk + possessive + için; noun/-DIk + possessive + -dan dolayı; noun/-DIk + possessive + -dan yüzünden
b2-cause-clauses.explanation: You've used çünkü to link two full sentences (Geldim çünkü seni özledim). -DIğI için packages the reason into a single clause using the -DIk participle you already know, placed BEFORE the result: 'Yorgun olduğum için erken yattım' (Because I was tired, I went to bed early). dolayı and yüzünden do the same job as postpositions after an ablative-marked noun or -DIk clause; yüzünden usually carries a negative flavor ('because of, due to the fault of'), while dolayı is neutral, more formal.
b2-cause-clauses.fact: yüzünden literally contains yüz (face) + possessive + -DAn (from its face/surface) — a vivid metaphor for 'on account of,' and its negative undertone comes from centuries of being used almost exclusively to blame something for a problem.
